newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's Imran dismisses child claim as plot.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's Imran dismisses child claim as plot.

text.p: Pakistan's former cricket hero and aspiring politician Imran Khan fended off questions on Wednesday about the source of his election warchest and allegations that he was the father of an illegitimate child.

"If anyone proves that I have taken even one paisa (one hundredth of a rupee) from the Jewish lobby, I am ready to leave politics and go to jail," he told reporters before kicking off his election campaign with a rally in Karachi.
Imran married Jemima Goldsmith, the daughter of wealthy Anglo-French financier Sir James Goldsmith, who is Jewish, in 1995. Jemima, a convert to Islam, gave birth to a son last year.
He was bombarded with queries about Sita White, a former girlfriend who filed a paternity suit in Los Angeles on Monday seeking to prove Imran fathered her four-year-old daughter.
Imran said he had known White for 10 years and his lawyers would deal with any legal action she might take when notified.
He accused former prime minister Nawaz Sharif, leader of the Pakistan Muslim League (PML) party, of deliberately manufacturing the issue before February 3 polls.
"The timing of the issue of Sita White clearly shows that a money game is being played," he said. "This is a plot."
Imran said that his Tehrik-i-Insaaf (Justice Movement) was up against what he called a political mafia with plenty of money and the power to intimidate potential opponents in rural areas.

Imran, a newcomer to politics, said more than 90 percent of his candidates had never fought elections before. He did not say how many of the 217 seats in the National Assembly (lower house) his nine-month-old party would contest.

Imran predicted that Tehrik-i-Insaaf would emerge as the "second force" in Pakistani politics after the elections, saying that the Pakistan People's Party (PPP) of ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto was unlikely to contest the polls.
"The atmosphere is not good for the PPP, which is facing much resentment from the people," he said. "But we are determined to contest elections and give light and hope to the people of Pakistan."

Imran, campaigning to cleanse Pakistani politics of corruption and combat foreign influence, said the present caretaker government led by Meraj Khalid had no mandate to introduce far-reaching reforms.
"We want to introduce wide-ranging reforms to the silent majority," he said.
He later told members of the Karachi Chamber of Commerce and Industry he would slash the size of government and give more freedom to traders if voted to power.
"We will go for a radical surgery to cut down not only the number of government departments and ministries but also the number of civil servants," he said in a speech.
"There is no justification in keeping 48 ministries in the centre when the government of India is being run by only 15 ministries," said Imran, who aspires to be the next prime minister.
"Previous prime ministers made the government an employment agency," he said.
President Farooq Leghari ordered national and provincial elections after he sacked Bhutto on charges of misrule and corruption on November 5. Bhutto denies the charges.
